title: Did we waste $500K on MBAs? Our honest take. EP 6
summary: A short mailbag episode where Cherie (Stanford GSB) and Jean (HBS) answer whether their combined half-million-dollar MBAs were worth it. Cherie went to fill deliberate gaps in knowledge, social life and confidence and came out more grounded; Jean went with a specific plan to build a startup during two 'risk-free' years and learned that entrepreneurship was right for her but that particular company was not. Both conclude it was worth it and Jean almost always tells people to go.

ideas.idea: The most noticeable change from business school is confidence and groundedness that third parties can hear in your voice.
ideas.detail: Cherie's best friends and classmates' former bosses said they sounded way more self-assured after; she attributes it to two years of reflection at GSB on who you are, what you care about and how you want to leave your impression on the world. Former coworkers scoff that 'a quarter million dollars for confidence' does not sound worth it.

ideas.idea: Business school teaches you enough to be dangerous in every field, so you can spot when something is totally off even if you never practice it yourself.
ideas.detail: Jean will never be an accountant but knows from her accounting class when numbers are wrong; a breadth of finance, econ, entertainment and accounting classes makes you more knowledgeable and confident as a person.

ideas.idea: Knowing the vocabulary of an industry puts you light years ahead and lets you walk into meetings unafraid and unlikely to be taken advantage of.
ideas.detail: Cherie's commercial real estate investing class, a 180 from her software and VC background, taught her to ask about foot traffic, vacancy rates, mall versus strip mall and proximity to hotels or airports if the sisters ever opened a cafe, even while still hiring a real estate lawyer or agent.

ideas.idea: Improv and play classes build comfort with your body in space and make you unafraid of being cringe, which feeds public speaking.
ideas.detail: Cherie took Stanford's 'The Spirit of Play' theater class on bringing playfulness into work and teams; she thinks it subconsciously helped her deliver a TED Talk and Jean credits her extemporaneous speaking ability.

ideas.idea: Go into business school intentionally with a list of specific gaps to fill, including social and community gaps, not just academic ones.
ideas.detail: After a lonely pandemic year living with her mom, Cherie, a longtime LinkedIn product manager with brief VC experience, wanted to grow socially, meet professors and add tools to her tool belt outside her existing expertise.

ideas.idea: Business school differs from other grad programs because everyone is bought into the social and community aspect as a core part of the value, not just academics.
ideas.detail: Jean's best friends at Harvard Law and the Harvard Ed School had far more academically oriented experiences; at HBS it is expected that you never eat dinner alone, which is why people joke MBAs party all the time.

ideas.idea: Introverts can thrive in business school by budgeting their emotional and mental capacity, including deliberately eating some dinners alone.
ideas.detail: Cherie ate many dinners alone to recover from full days of socializing; she says she has many introvert friends who found their balance, and this is worth self-reflection before applying.

ideas.idea: Business school can be two risk-free years to build a startup with a built-in downside case: if it fails, you still graduate with the degree.
ideas.detail: Jean lacked the chutzpah to quit her job and applied partly because her GMAT score was expiring after five years; she chose HBS for its entrepreneurship push via the Harvard Innovation Lab, a reaction to Stanford's strength, planning to build in year one, go full time in summer, get customers and fundraise at graduation.

ideas.idea: Trying entrepreneurship in a supportive cohort taught Jean that she loves building companies but that the specific startup was not worth the next 5-10 years, which was itself a valuable result.
ideas.detail: She worked on the startup heavily in year one at the expense of classes and social life, intentionally; she notes programs like Y Combinator and South Park Commons now offer similar cohort experiences outside school.

ideas.idea: The $250,000 tuition plus lost salary is worth it if you believe in yourself, because a long career lets you recoup the money and an environment where your only job is to learn is rare.
ideas.detail: Jean does not like to think about the opportunity cost because it is depressing, but she almost always says yes when people ask whether to go; a future episode could cover who should not go.
